data.name: Sickness
data.detailed_description:
Stats (September 25th 2017)
Word count: 216,000 words
Number of CGs: 85 (plus variations of several)
Number of sprites: 32 (mostly minor characters)
31 original music tracks, + 9 CCA-by tracks



Summary/Plot

Sickness is a Visual Novel following the life of Suoh, a high school student turned violent criminal.

Following the deaths of his parents, Suoh is left without a home or source of income. All he has is his twin sister, Sara, who he promises to provide for, even if doing so means throwing his life away.

Using the entirety of their savings, the two move to another city, wherein Suoh quickly finds work. Sara commutes to her old school, Suoh works long, physically-demanding hours, and the two survive off instant food, barely scraping by. It isn't a happy life, but they make it work.

Or at least they did, until a violent outburst set into motion a rapid descent.

Amid a physical altercation with his boss, Suoh blacks out, waking up to find a corpse laying at his feet. His knuckles bloody, his muscles aching, he realizes that he has just murdered his boss, the person responsible for his continued well-being. But rather than lament the loss of life, all Suoh can think of is how badly he needed the money, and what he'll do next to get it.

Drawn by the scent of blood, one of Suoh's coworkers, a young man with criminal connections, offers him a not so legal revenue stream, one encouraging violent behavior and rewarding the capable.

And from there, everything spirals out of control.

As it turns out, Suoh has a knack for crime, and the petty reservations he had about such acts don't last long. For the well-being of his sister, as well as his own self-interest, he becomes a killer for hire, taking out people anybody his new boss tells him to. He quickly adapts to life as a killer, adopting a double life his sister can never know about.

But his new life is not without trouble. Facing death on a weekly basis is only the beginning; between avoiding police detection, eyewitnesses, and even the malice of his fellow professional killers, Suoh's new life looks to be the death of him.

Will Suoh manage to survive long enough to keep his promise to his sister? Will he turn tail and escape from this life of crime, finding solace in the company of someone or something else? Or will he be hunted down and killed before he ever gets the chance?


Main Characters

Sara Tesla - Suoh's twin sister

Sara is a high school student who harbors complex feelings. To her brother, Sara is an angelic sister with a loving nature and endless affection; an image she cultivates and builds on daily. To everyone else, however, Sara is narcissistic and thoroughly two-faced.
Family aside, Sara doesn't care for other people in the slightest, and as a result of her desperately trying to hide this fact, her family mistakenly believe Sara to be bipolar.


Karasu - An up and coming crimelord

Karasu builds his wealth through a variety of "services", including, but not limited to, gambling, corporate espionage, and organ trafficking. Above all, however, Karasu is most famous for providing "waste disposal" for neighboring towns, whether they request his services or not.
His ultimate goal is to build an empire he can share with his beloved "children"; interesting individuals he has taken under his wing and granted a new lease on life.
Though many view him as a sadistic narcissist who will stop at nothing to obtain what he wants, Karasu is ultimately a simple businessman who displays affection only for a chosen few.


Sai - Karasu's right-hand man

Sai is Karasu's most trusted and capable employee, responsible for overseeing his most lucrative business ventures, despite always working in the shadows. He is also responsible for “breaking in” new recruits, and as such becomes Suoh's teacher.
Unrivaled in what he does, Sai is a ruthless killer who feels no remorse; those who get on his bad side seldom live long enough to realize it.
The only things more important to Sai than his work are his daughter's well-being and happiness.


Misa - Sai's daughter

Misa is a teenage girl who wishes for a normal life.
Being the daughter of a professional killer (and protective father), however, Misa has trained from a young age in order to protect herself from the dangers of the world, and in doing so inevitably became aware of her father's line of work.
As her father's work absorbed her life, Misa adapted her skillset to match those of a killer, using her youth and small figure to become the youngest and most discreet killer among her peers.
Outside of work, Misa is still just a young girl. She's very friendly, once she warms up to someone, and is protective of those close to her.

data.short_description: Sickness is a visual novel centering around Suoh Tesla, an amoral high school student whose life is rapidly deteriorating. Following the deaths of his parents, a brief stay in the hospital, and the emergence of his “Sickness”, his daily life quickly devolves from carefree school days to a life of crime.

reviews.review:
Sickness is a dark psychological visual novel that explores desperation, violence, emotional instability, and the gradual destruction of personal morality. Developed by Zetsubou and published by Unwonted Studios and Zetsubou, the game offers an unsettling narrative that challenges conventional expectations of character-driven storytelling. Instead of presenting a heroic adventure, it follows a troubled individual whose increasingly questionable decisions expose the disturbing consequences of survival instincts and moral compromise. Its mature themes, complicated relationships, and oppressive atmosphere make it particularly appealing to readers who appreciate psychological thrillers and unconventional crime dramas.

The story follows Suoh Tesla, a young man whose life deteriorates after losing his parents and developing a mysterious condition that influences his behavior. Struggling financially while attempting to support his twin sister, Sara, Suoh becomes involved in criminal activities that gradually transform his personality and worldview. His descent into violence forms the foundation of the narrative, presenting situations where desperation and personal responsibility become increasingly difficult to distinguish. Rather than encouraging players to admire him, the story challenges them to understand how circumstances, emotional instability, and repeated moral compromises can turn an ordinary individual into someone capable of disturbing actions.

Character development is among the game's strongest qualities. Suoh's complicated personality makes him an intriguing protagonist despite his frequently reprehensible behavior. His relationship with Sara introduces themes of family loyalty, emotional dependence, and unhealthy attachment. Supporting characters, including the experienced assassin Sai and his daughter Misa, contribute additional perspectives on violence, responsibility, and human relationships. Their contrasting personalities create moments of unexpected warmth within an otherwise disturbing environment. These interactions provide emotional variety while reinforcing the idea that individuals involved in criminal activities can possess surprisingly complicated personal motivations.

The writing emphasizes psychological tension, moral ambiguity, and the consequences of destructive choices. Conversations and internal reflections frequently reveal the characters' insecurities, motivations, and emotional contradictions. Rather than depending entirely on graphic violence, the narrative develops much of its atmosphere through uncomfortable situations and increasingly unstable relationships. Nevertheless, certain developments feel exaggerated, while some emotional transitions lack sufficient buildup. The story occasionally prioritizes shocking circumstances over subtle characterization, which can weaken its dramatic effectiveness. Despite these shortcomings, its willingness to examine morally uncomfortable subjects gives the experience a distinctive identity.

Gameplay follows the traditional visual novel structure, emphasizing extensive reading, dialogue sequences, and occasional decisions that influence narrative progression. Different choices can lead toward alternative developments and endings, encouraging players to revisit the story and examine its characters from different perspectives. Additional unlockable content further expands the narrative beyond its principal storyline. However, interactive mechanics remain limited, making this experience considerably more suitable for readers than players seeking action, exploration, or strategic challenges. Its entertainment value depends primarily on the strength of its storytelling and the player's investment in its characters.

With approximately 216,000 words of narrative content, Sickness provides substantial material for players who enjoy lengthy visual novels. This considerable scope allows relationships and psychological conflicts to develop across numerous conversations and dramatic encounters. However, the extensive script occasionally creates pacing problems. Some sequences maintain suspense effectively, while others spend excessive time on relatively minor interactions. Although these quieter passages contribute to characterization, they sometimes interrupt the momentum of the central storyline. Readers who appreciate detailed character development will likely find the slower sections more rewarding than those expecting continuous dramatic revelations.

Visually, the game uses anime-inspired character artwork, illustrated story scenes, and conventional visual novel presentation techniques. Character sprites effectively communicate emotional reactions, while special illustrations highlight significant narrative developments. The contrast between appealing character designs and disturbing subject matter creates an unusual atmosphere. Although the artwork serves its purpose, the production lacks the elaborate animation and visual sophistication of higher-budget releases. Backgrounds and transitions are generally functional, placing greater emphasis on dialogue and narrative imagination than visual spectacle.

The soundtrack complements the psychological atmosphere through music that supports moments of suspense, emotional vulnerability, and confrontation. Its compositions help distinguish quieter interpersonal scenes from increasingly dangerous situations. Without full voice acting, emotional expression depends largely on the written dialogue, character portraits, and musical accompaniment. This traditional approach works reasonably well, although players accustomed to fully voiced visual novels may find the presentation comparatively restrained. The mature content also deserves consideration, as the narrative includes violence, psychological distress, suicide-related themes, and disturbing family relationships that may be uncomfortable for some audiences.

Regarding technical accessibility, Sickness supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, alongside Steam achievements, trading cards, and cloud saving. Its Steam Deck compatibility is officially classified as Verified, making it suitable for handheld play. Controller compatibility improvements and updates addressing earlier Steam Deck issues further support its portable accessibility. The straightforward reading-focused interface is particularly appropriate for players who prefer experiencing visual novels in shorter sessions without requiring demanding gameplay interactions.

Overall, Sickness is a compelling psychological crime visual novel that succeeds through its morally complex protagonist, substantial narrative content, disturbing atmosphere, and unconventional character relationships. Its exploration of desperation and emotional corruption provides a memorable experience, even when inconsistent pacing and occasional melodrama undermine its storytelling ambitions. While its limited interactivity and unsettling subject matter restrict its mainstream appeal, mature audiences interested in dark, character-driven fiction will discover an engaging narrative with meaningful replay value. Despite its imperfections, the game remains a distinctive contribution to independent visual novel storytelling. 

Rating: 8/10
